e: A muscle can only shorten so far. Rectus femoris runs from the iliac bone to the tibia via the patella, so sitting with the hip flexed has already used up part of its available shortening. That is active insufficiency, and it is why the other three quadriceps, which cross only the knee, do relatively more work in a seated leg extension.

q: Gastrocnemius originates on the posterior femur, above the knee. What follows for a calf raise performed with the knee bent?
o: Gastrocnemius contributes less, so the work shifts toward soleus
Gastrocnemius contributes more, because the knee flexion pre-stretches it
Nothing changes, since both muscles insert on the calcaneus
The Achilles tendon takes the load instead of either muscle
e: Bending the knee brings the femoral origin closer to the calcaneus, slackening gastrocnemius before the movement starts. Soleus originates below the knee on the tibia and fibula, so it is unaffected. That is the whole logic of the seated calf raise: it is not a different exercise so much as a way of removing one of the two muscles.

q: Why is it difficult to produce maximal hip extension and maximal knee flexion at the same moment?
o: The hamstrings cross both joints, so both actions shorten the same muscle at once
The hip and knee are controlled by antagonistic reflex arcs
Gluteus maximus inhibits the hamstrings during knee flexion
The rectus femoris blocks the knee from flexing fully under load
e: Biceps femoris long head, semimembranosus and semitendinosus all run from the ischial tuberosity past the knee. Extending the hip shortens them at one end and flexing the knee shortens them at the other, so the muscle runs out of range. It is why a stiff-legged deadlift and a leg curl train the same muscles in genuinely different ways.

q: Biceps femoris short head originates on the linea aspera of the femur rather than the pelvis. What does that mean it cannot do?
o: Extend the hip
Flex the knee
Externally rotate the tibia
Stabilise the knee
e: A muscle can only act on joints its line of pull crosses. The short head starts on the femur itself, below the hip, so the hip is not in its path at all. It flexes the knee and externally rotates the tibia like the long head, but it is the one part of the hamstring complex that does nothing for hip extension.

q: The long head of triceps brachii originates on the scapula rather than the humerus. What follows for an overhead triceps extension?
o: It is stretched at the shoulder, which lengthens it before the elbow extends
It is switched off, so only the medial and lateral heads work
It becomes a shoulder abductor rather than an elbow extensor
It loses all leverage at the elbow once the arm is overhead
e: Raising the arm overhead moves the scapular origin away from the ulna, putting the long head on stretch before the set begins. That is the argument for overhead variations: the head that crosses the shoulder is the one that is loaded differently by arm position, while the other two heads are unaffected.

q: Biceps brachii originates on the scapula, not the humerus. What does that add to its job list beyond the elbow and forearm?
o: Shoulder flexion
Shoulder abduction
Scapular retraction
Shoulder external rotation
e: Crossing the shoulder gives it a third action. Biceps flexes the elbow, supinates the forearm and assists shoulder flexion, which is why a preacher curl with the upper arm fixed feels different from a standing curl where the shoulder is free to contribute.

q: Gluteus maximus inserts partly into the iliotibial band, which runs down to the tibia. What does that let it influence?
o: Tibial internal rotation, which it decelerates
Ankle plantar flexion
Knee extension torque directly
Patellar tracking through the quadriceps tendon
e: Most of glute max inserts on the femur, but the fibres running into the iliotibial band continue past the knee. That is how a hip muscle ends up controlling rotation at the tibia, and it is the mechanical basis for treating weak glutes as a knee problem rather than only a hip one.

q: Tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus both insert into the iliotibial band. How do their hip actions compare?
o: They oppose each other: TFL flexes and internally rotates, glute max extends and externally rotates
They are synergists, both extending and externally rotating the hip
They are synergists, both flexing and internally rotating the hip
TFL abducts and glute max adducts, with no rotational difference
e: A shared insertion does not mean a shared action; what matters is where each one starts. TFL comes off the ilium in front of the hip, glute max from behind it. So the same band is tensioned from two opposite directions, which is why the pairing shows up constantly in discussions of lateral knee pain.

q: Sartorius runs from the iliac bone across the thigh to the medial tibia. Which combination does that diagonal line produce?
o: Hip flexion, external rotation and abduction, with knee flexion
Hip extension, internal rotation and adduction, with knee extension
Hip flexion, internal rotation and adduction, with knee extension
Hip abduction and internal rotation, with knee extension
e: Trace the line and the answer falls out. It starts in front of and outside the hip and finishes inside the knee, so shortening it flexes, externally rotates and abducts the hip while flexing the knee. That is the position of sitting cross-legged, which is where its name comes from: it is the tailor's muscle.

q: Gracilis is the only adductor that reaches past the knee, inserting on the medial tibia. What does that add?
o: It assists knee flexion and tibial internal rotation
It assists knee extension
It produces ankle inversion
It has no action beyond the hip despite the insertion
e: Every other adductor stops on the femur, so it can only act at the hip. Gracilis carries on to the tibia, which is why it turns up in the knee flexor list as well and why adductor strains sometimes present with symptoms nearer the knee than expected.

q: Gluteus medius has anterior and posterior fibres with opposite rotational actions. What produces that split?
o: The fibres sit on either side of the hip's axis of rotation, so they pull in opposite directions
The anterior and posterior fibres have different nerve supplies
The posterior fibres attach to the sacrum rather than the ilium
Only the anterior fibres cross the joint
e: Both sets abduct, because both run from the ilium down to the greater trochanter. But the anterior fibres lie in front of the rotational axis and the posterior fibres behind it, so one internally rotates and the other externally rotates. One muscle, two opposed jobs, decided by geometry.

q: Adductor magnus is often described as having a hamstring part. Which fibres earn that description and why?
o: The posterior fibres, which extend and externally rotate the hip rather than flexing and internally rotating it
The anterior fibres, because they attach nearest the ischium
All of it, because the whole muscle crosses the knee
Neither: the name refers only to its size
e: The posterior fibres run from nearer the ischial tuberosity down the back of the femur, which is the hamstring line of pull. They adduct like the rest of the muscle but extend the hip where the anterior fibres flex it, so the same muscle appears on both sides of the hip action list.

q: External oblique produces contralateral rotation and internal oblique ipsilateral rotation. What explains the difference?
o: Their fibres run in opposite diagonals, so each pulls the trunk toward a different side
The external oblique is stronger, so it dominates the direction
Internal oblique attaches to the spine and external oblique does not
The difference is in timing rather than direction
e: External oblique runs downward and forward, internal oblique downward and backward, forming an X across the abdomen. Rotating left uses the right external oblique together with the left internal oblique. They work as diagonal pairs, which is why trunk rotation is never a one-muscle job.

q: Transversus abdominis runs horizontally and inserts into the linea alba. What follows for what it can do?
o: It cannot move the spine at all; it can only compress
It rotates the spine more powerfully than the obliques
It flexes the spine but cannot extend it
It laterally flexes the spine only
e: Movement needs a line of pull that crosses a joint at an angle to it. TVA wraps round the abdomen and ends in a midline seam, so shortening it draws the waist inward and raises intra-abdominal pressure. That is why it is the flagship stabilisation muscle and why it is trained with the drawing-in manoeuvre rather than with any movement.

q: Rectus abdominis has vertical fibres running from pubis to ribs. Why is it a poor rotator despite appearing in the rotation column?
o: A vertical line of pull sits almost along the spine's rotational axis, so it has very little leverage for twisting
It is separated by tendinous intersections, which prevent rotation
It is too superficial to reach the vertebrae
It only rotates when the obliques are inhibited
e: Flexion is what a vertical anterior line does well: it draws the ribs toward the pubis directly. Rotation needs a diagonal, which is what the obliques supply. The tables list rotation for rectus abdominis, but the geometry says it is a minor contributor.

q: Pectoralis major has clavicular and sternal fibres. What does the split mean in practice?
o: The clavicular fibres are better placed for shoulder flexion, the sternal fibres for horizontal adduction from a lower angle
The clavicular fibres internally rotate and the sternal fibres externally rotate
Only the sternal fibres cross the shoulder joint
The two parts have identical actions but different nerve supplies
e: Both converge on the anterior humerus, but one starts high on the clavicle and the other low on the sternum and ribs. The angle of pull differs, which is the honest mechanical basis for incline versus flat pressing, rather than a claim about training an upper or lower half of a single sheet.

q: Serratus anterior and the rhomboids act on the same bone in opposite directions. What is the pairing?
o: Serratus protracts and upwardly rotates the scapula; the rhomboids retract and downwardly rotate it
Serratus elevates and the rhomboids depress the scapula
Serratus retracts and the rhomboids protract the scapula
Both protract, differing only in the degree of upward rotation
e: Serratus runs from the ribs round to the front of the scapula and pulls it forward round the ribcage. The rhomboids run from the thoracic spine to the medial border and pull it back and down. Overhead pressing needs the first; rowing emphasises the second.

q: Supraspinatus and the lateral deltoid both abduct the arm. What distinguishes their contributions?
o: Supraspinatus initiates the movement, where the deltoid's line of pull has little leverage
The deltoid initiates and supraspinatus finishes the last portion
Supraspinatus works only above shoulder height
They are interchangeable, which is why cuff tears rarely affect abduction
e: With the arm at the side the deltoid pulls almost straight up the humerus, which compresses rather than rotates the joint. Supraspinatus sits above the joint and can start the movement, after which the deltoid gains leverage. That is why a cuff tear often shows up as difficulty starting a lift rather than finishing one.

q: Three of the four rotator cuff muscles externally rotate or abduct. Which is the exception and why?
o: Subscapularis, because it is the only one attaching to the anterior surface of the scapula
Supraspinatus, because it passes under the acromion
Teres minor, because it attaches lowest on the scapula
Infraspinatus, because its fibres run horizontally
e: Position decides action. Teres minor and infraspinatus lie on the back of the scapula and pull the humerus into external rotation; supraspinatus sits on top and abducts. Subscapularis is on the front, between scapula and ribcage, so it is the cuff's internal rotator and the only anterior one.

q: Anterior and posterior deltoid share an insertion on the humerus but oppose each other. Which pair of actions separates them?
o: Anterior flexes and internally rotates; posterior extends and externally rotates
Anterior abducts and posterior adducts
Anterior externally rotates and posterior internally rotates
Anterior elevates the scapula and posterior depresses it
e: The three heads are one muscle only by name. The anterior head comes off the clavicle in front of the joint and the posterior head off the scapular spine behind it, so they sit on opposite sides of the axis and do opposite things. The middle head, directly lateral, abducts.

q: Latissimus dorsi runs from the lumbar spine, iliac crest and thoracic spine to the anterior humerus. What does that unusual span let it do?
o: Connect the arm to the pelvis, so it also decelerates spinal flexion
Rotate the lumbar spine as its primary role
Elevate the scapula
Act as a hip extensor through a direct femoral attachment
e: Almost nothing else in the body bridges the pelvis to the humerus. That span is why a tight lat limits overhead reach by tethering the arm to the trunk, and why it appears in the spinal deceleration column despite being thought of as an arm muscle.

q: Teres major is sometimes called the lat's little helper. What does it share, and what does it lack?
o: The same shoulder actions, but no attachment to the spine or pelvis
The same spinal attachments, but no humeral insertion
The same actions plus scapular retraction
The same origin, but opposite rotational action
e: Both insert on the anterior humerus and both extend, adduct and internally rotate the shoulder. Teres major starts on the scapula rather than the spine and pelvis, so it does the arm half of the job without any of the trunk connection.

q: Fibularis longus starts on the lateral fibula but inserts on the medial side of the foot. How does it evert?
o: Its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus, which acts as a pulley and reverses the direction of pull
It changes direction inside the ankle joint capsule
It everts only when posterior tibialis is inactive
The medial insertion is a naming convention rather than a real attachment
e: The straight line from origin to insertion is not the line of pull; the tendon's path is. Wrapping behind the lateral malleolus and under the foot turns a laterally placed muscle into one that pulls the medial side downward, which is eversion. Bony pulleys change actions, so attachments alone can mislead.

q: Posterior tibialis and fibularis longus both attach near the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal, yet oppose each other. Why?
o: They approach from opposite sides of the ankle, so their tendons pull the same bones in opposite directions
One inserts on bone and the other on fascia
Posterior tibialis acts only during gait
Their actions are identical and the tables disagree
e: Posterior tibialis passes behind the medial malleolus and inverts; fibularis longus passes behind the lateral malleolus and everts. Shared insertion, opposite approach, opposite action. Together they form a stirrup under the arch, which is why both are listed as stabilising it.

q: Soleus originates below the knee, on the tibia and fibula. What does that make it well suited to?
o: Postural work at the ankle regardless of knee position
Producing power only when the knee is fully extended
Assisting knee flexion during running
Controlling the arch during pronation
e: Because it does not cross the knee, its length is unaffected by whether you are standing, sitting or squatting. That independence is why it carries much of the continuous, low-level work of holding the body upright over the ankles.

q: Anterior tibialis runs down the front of the shin to the medial cuneiform. What is its most common eccentric job in walking?
o: Controlling the foot's descent to the ground after heel strike
Driving push-off at the end of stance
Holding the knee extended through mid-stance
Resisting eversion during the swing phase
e: It accelerates dorsiflexion and inversion, so lengthening under load it controls the opposite. After the heel lands, the forefoot would slap down under gravity; anterior tibialis pays out to lower it. That eccentric role is why shin pain so often follows a sharp increase in walking or running volume.

q: Quadratus lumborum runs from the iliac crest to the 12th rib and lumbar vertebrae. What does shortening it on one side do to the pelvis?
o: Hitches that side of the pelvis upward and laterally flexes the spine toward the same side
Drops that side of the pelvis and laterally flexes away
Rotates the pelvis toward the opposite side
Tilts the pelvis anteriorly without lateral movement
e: Either end can be the moving one. Fix the ribs and the pelvis rises on that side; fix the pelvis and the spine bends toward it. Both are the same shortening, and which one you see depends on what is anchored, which is a general rule worth carrying to every muscle.

q: Levator scapulae attaches the cervical spine to the scapula. Why does the tables list two quite different sets of actions for it?
o: Either end can be the anchor, so it moves the neck when the scapula is fixed and the scapula when the neck is fixed
It has two separate bellies with different innervation
The action depends on whether the head is rotated
One set is concentric and the other is a different muscle's
e: A muscle pulls both of its ends toward each other. Whichever end is held still becomes the origin for that moment. With the shoulder anchored it extends and side-bends the neck; with the neck anchored it elevates and downwardly rotates the scapula. Same contraction, different anchor.

q: Scalenes run from the cervical vertebrae to the first and second ribs. What does that give them besides neck movement?
o: A role in inhalation, by elevating the upper ribs
A role in swallowing
Scapular elevation
Thoracic rotation
e: Anything attaching to a rib can move it. With the neck fixed, the scalenes lift the first two ribs, which assists inspiration. That is why they are often tight in people who breathe shallowly into the upper chest, and why neck symptoms and breathing pattern are worth considering together.

q: Erector spinae accelerate spinal extension. What are they doing during the lowering phase of a hip hinge?
o: Lengthening under load to decelerate spinal flexion and hold position
Shortening to drive the movement downward
Relaxing, since gravity produces the movement
Working isometrically only at the very bottom
e: Gravity supplies the downward movement, so the muscles that would extend the spine are the ones paying out to stop it flexing. That is the whole job of the back in a deadlift or a good morning: it is an isometric and eccentric task, not a concentric one.

q: Multifidus produces spinal extension and contralateral rotation. What makes it suited to segmental control rather than gross movement?
o: It spans only a few vertebrae at a time, so it controls one segment against the next
It is the largest of the spinal extensors
It attaches to the ribs rather than the vertebrae
It contracts only during rotation
e: Short muscles crossing few joints are positioned for fine control rather than large movement, in the same way the rotator cuff is positioned relative to the deltoid. Multifidus is why segmental stability and gross trunk strength are different qualities.

q: Psoas originates on the lumbar spine rather than the pelvis. What consequence does that have that iliacus does not share?
o: Contracting it pulls on the lumbar spine as well as the femur
It cannot flex the hip without the knee also flexing
It externally rotates the hip where iliacus internally rotates it
It has no effect on the femur at all
e: Iliacus runs from the iliac fossa to the femur, so it acts only at the hip. Psoas starts on the lumbar vertebrae, so tension in it reaches the low back. That is the anatomical basis for the link commonly drawn between tight hip flexors and lumbar position, and the reason the two muscles are worth distinguishing despite the shared tendon.

q: Piriformis extends, abducts and externally rotates the hip in neutral. Why is it sometimes described as changing role in deep hip flexion?
o: Deep flexion moves its line of pull across the joint axis, so it can act as an internal rotator instead
It becomes inactive beyond ninety degrees of flexion
It converts from a stabiliser to a prime mover
The sciatic nerve blocks it mechanically
e: Its action depends on where the femur sits relative to the muscle. Flex the hip far enough and the same line of pull arrives on the other side of the axis, reversing what it does. This is a good reminder that muscle actions are stated for anatomical position and are not fixed properties.

q: Brachialis runs from the humerus to the ulna. Why is it unaffected by whether the forearm is supinated or pronated?
o: The ulna does not rotate during pronation and supination, so its line of pull is unchanged
It is too deep to be influenced by forearm position
It crosses the shoulder, which compensates
Its tendon rotates with the radius to compensate
e: Pronation and supination are the radius crossing over a relatively fixed ulna. Biceps inserts on the radius, so forearm position changes its leverage; brachialis inserts on the ulna and is therefore a pure elbow flexor in any grip. That is the reasoning behind the hammer and reverse curl.

q: Brachioradialis runs from the humerus to the distal radius. In which forearm position is it best placed to flex the elbow?
o: Neutral, with the thumb upward
Fully supinated, palm upward
Fully pronated, palm downward
Position makes no difference to it
e: Its line of pull is most favourable when the forearm is midway between pronation and supination, which is why a hammer curl loads it more than a standard curl. Attachment sites explain grip choices more reliably than exercise names do.

q: Semitendinosus and semimembranosus internally rotate the tibia, while biceps femoris externally rotates it. What explains the split?
o: The two medial hamstrings insert on the medial tibia and biceps femoris on the lateral fibula
They have different origins on the ischium
Biceps femoris crosses the hip and the others do not
Only biceps femoris crosses the knee
e: All three descend from the ischium, but they finish on opposite sides of the knee. A medial insertion turns the tibia inward when it shortens; a lateral one turns it outward. Insertion side decides rotation, which is derivable without memorising it.

q: Three of the four quadriceps originate on the femur and one on the pelvis. What single difference does that create?
o: Only rectus femoris can flex the hip
Only rectus femoris can extend the knee
The vastii cannot stabilise the knee
Rectus femoris cannot contribute to knee extension
e: All four converge on the patella and extend the knee. Rectus femoris is the only one whose origin lies above the hip, so it is the only one that crosses two joints and the only one that flexes the hip. Everything distinctive about it follows from that one attachment.

q: Upper trapezius attaches to the occipital bone and C7 at one end and the clavicle and acromion at the other. What two regions can it therefore act on?
o: The cervical spine and the scapula
The cervical spine and the humerus
The scapula and the ribcage
The thoracic spine and the humerus
e: It spans from skull and neck to shoulder girdle, so it appears in both lists: cervical extension, lateral flexion and rotation, and scapular elevation. A muscle that crosses two regions has a job in each, and which one moves depends on which end is anchored.

q: Pectoralis minor runs from the ribs to the coracoid process of the scapula. What does shortening it do?
o: Draws the scapula forward and down into protraction
Retracts and elevates the scapula
Internally rotates the humerus
Flexes the shoulder
e: It never touches the humerus, so it cannot move the arm directly. It acts on the scapula, pulling the coracoid toward the ribs. That is why a short pec minor is discussed as a postural issue at the shoulder blade rather than as chest strength.

q: Which muscle would you expect to decelerate hip adduction during single-leg stance?
o: Gluteus medius
Adductor longus
Psoas
Piriformis
e: Standing on one leg, the unsupported side of the pelvis tends to drop, which is adduction at the stance hip. The abductors are what resist it, and gluteus medius is the main one. This is the mechanism behind the Trendelenburg sign and the reason single-leg work exposes it.

q: Which muscle would be lengthening under load during the cocking phase of a throw, as the shoulder externally rotates to its limit?
o: Subscapularis
Infraspinatus
Teres minor
Posterior deltoid
e: External rotation is being produced, so the muscles that internally rotate are the ones paying out to control it. Subscapularis is the cuff's internal rotator, which is why it is loaded eccentrically at the end of the cocking phase and why it features in throwing injuries.

q: Rotating the trunk to the left uses which oblique pair?
o: Right external oblique with left internal oblique
Left external oblique with left internal oblique
Right external oblique with right internal oblique
Left external oblique with right internal oblique
e: External oblique produces contralateral rotation, so turning left uses the right one. Internal oblique produces ipsilateral rotation, so it is the left one. The pair forms a continuous diagonal across the front of the trunk, which is why rotation is always a two-sided action.

q: A client reports calf tightness that eases when they sit but returns on standing. Which muscle does the attachment anatomy point toward?
o: Soleus, because it does not cross the knee and so is unaffected by sitting
Gastrocnemius, because sitting shortens it at the femur
Anterior tibialis, because it works hardest in standing
Fibularis longus, because it stabilises the arch
e: Read the symptom against the attachments. Sitting flexes the knee, which slackens gastrocnemius but does nothing to soleus. If the sensation persists in standing and eases in sitting, the muscle whose length changed is gastrocnemius. Attachment reasoning is a diagnostic tool, not just an exam topic.

q: Which attachment detail explains why the hip flexors are described as tilting the pelvis anteriorly?
o: They attach to the pelvis and lumbar spine above and the femur below, so with the leg fixed they pull the pelvis forward and down
They insert on the sacrum, which rotates the whole pelvis
They attach to the iliotibial band, which tilts the ilium
They pull the pubic bone upward toward the ribs
e: With the femur planted, the moving end is the pelvis. Iliacus and psoas run from the ilium and lumbar spine to the femur, so shortening them rolls the top of the pelvis forward. Same contraction as hip flexion, different anchored end.
